note: Lucas reviewed 46 flagged principles on 2026-10-28. Every principle in research/01-03 not listed here is kept as written. 02-writing.md section 13 (muted viewer) is kept in full. final.action is binding.

items.why_flagged: Too strict for news on stills: muted viewers get the story from the captions, and a photo rarely carries plot by itself.
A silent gap is dead air for a muted viewer, and long gaps cost retention.
Stills have no natural sound, and silence as a throttle never reaches a muted viewer. W-34 covers what is left.
Same reason as W-34.
Works for sound-on viewers only if something on screen holds the moment.

final.text: A beat with no narration before the key line, while the picture or on-screen words hold the moment.

items.why_flagged: Sound-first reveals are lost on mute.

final.text: Bring a new image in first and let it land for a moment, then name it.

items.why_flagged: Spoken signposts spend scarce words, and on-screen change does the job for both audiences.
Same as W-19.
Keep the idea, drop the spoken signpost.

final.text: Flag what matters with a change of pace and on-screen emphasis.

items.theme: What may be done to a real photo
items.why_flagged: AP allows only technical edits. Our cutouts, grade, grain and duotone would all break this.

final.text: Never change what a photo shows. Stylized treatment (cutout, grade, grain, duotone, blur behind a lifted subject) is allowed when it reads as treatment.

items.theme: What may be done to a real photo
items.why_flagged: Lifting a subject out of its background is removal, read literally.

final.text: Never add, remove, move or clone anything inside a photo's scene; lifting a subject out as a visible cutout is a treatment, not an edit.

items.theme: What may be done to a real photo
items.why_flagged: Forbids background blur and toning, which the documentary look uses. The D-73 rewrite covers the real limit.

items.theme: What may be done to a real photo
items.why_flagged: Parallax needs pixels filled in behind a lifted layer, which is a small use of image generation. You allowed generation in three cases and upscaling sparingly; this would be a fourth.

final.text: Use parallax on key images only. Filling the gap behind a lifted layer is allowed; inventing visible content is not.

items.theme: What may be done to a real photo
items.why_flagged: Labeling every posed or handout photo clutters 60 seconds. The on-screen credit and source log cover provenance.

items.theme: What may be done to a real photo
items.why_flagged: Superseded by your rule (MD-02): any photo without a watermark is usable. The source log (D-63) stays.
Searching for a bigger theme tends to end in a lesson.

final.text: Set the story inside the larger forces shaping AI; that context runs through it rather than arriving as a closing lesson. (Lucas: "I want these stories to be cognizant of the greater themes that are going on in the AI world. We don't necessarily need to end on a lesson or moral, but the story will probably be intertwined with a greater context.")

items.why_flagged: Same risk as D-6.

final.text: Give meaning in at most one line, as stakes, not a moral.

items.why_flagged: A reflection-line ending is a soft moral. Your ending is the thread that is still unfolding (MD-05).
An "explanatory narrative" is the educational format. The visuals check and selection pick stories that already have action.
Written for months of shooting. Our writer works from a finished fact sheet.

items.theme: Heroes, villains and whom the story centers
items.why_flagged: Rules out stories built around a flawed CEO or a rivalry, which are the core of AI drama.

items.theme: Heroes, villains and whom the story centers

items.theme: Heroes, villains and whom the story centers
items.why_flagged: In AI news the one at fault is often the protagonist. The Tinder Swindler rule doesn't map.

final.text: Never glorify wrongdoing; when people were harmed, give them their place in the story.

items.theme: Heroes, villains and whom the story centers
items.why_flagged: Covered by the D-33 rewrite.

items.theme: Heroes, villains and whom the story centers
items.why_flagged: We can't contact the subjects of a story.

final.text: When someone faces allegations, include their public response or denial if one exists.

items.why_flagged: It says 110–140 words while S-39 says 150–170 wpm. Your old pacing rule was 180–200 wpm with pauses of 0.2s or less.

final.text: Budget about 140–170 narrated words for 60 seconds, leaving room for two or three short picture beats.

items.why_flagged: Merged into the W-86 rewrite.
The format is 60 seconds. One unverified note says TikTok pays creators only on videos over a minute.

final.text: Aim for about 60 seconds; run up to about 75 only when the story needs it.

items.theme: Holding a still vs keeping it moving
items.why_flagged: Ken Burns lets key images hold, while short-form evidence says a frozen frame loses the eye (S-52, S-91).
Stills have no native sound, and short-form evidence says score from the start (S-70).
Burns layers ambience under stills. Your rule (RC-46) is that every sound is an on-screen action's own sound. Ambience is the open question.

items.why_flagged: Keep the voice consistent, but there's no spoken sign-off in this format.
Full-screen documents, posts and clippings are core evidence for us. The platform rule is about overlay text.
"Restrained graphics" vs the muted viewer's need for on-screen words.

final.text: Keep graphics restrained in style; on-screen words are there for the muted viewer and the evidence, never as decoration.

items.why_flagged: Two sources for every claim is strict. The old fact gate rejected 4 of 7 stories.

final.text: Confirm the claims the story turns on against two independent sources; supporting details need one reliable source.
